extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards for what subject-matter is patentable (novelty, utility, form vs principle, claims construction, and scope of appropriation of natural laws/qualities). Targets assessment and drafting of patent applications and court construction of patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject must be new and useful
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act requires that the subject of every patent should be "new and useful," whether it be an art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or an improvement on any of these things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This threshold question underlies the inquiry into what constitutes novelty and utility in the sense of the statute; applies to all listed categories and their improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: No patent for mere philosophical or abstract theory; must be reduced to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent cannot be obtained for a mere philosophical or abstract theory; it can only be for theory reduced to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is an art, it must be actually put in practice and unknown before; if a machine, it must be substantially new in structure and mode of operation and not merely changed in form or proportions; if a manufacture or composition, it must be something actually made and substantially different from anything previously known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty in machinery requires new mode/method/application of mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent is claimed for a whole machine, it must in substance be a new machine — a new mode, method, or application of mechanism to produce some new effect, or to produce an old effect in a new way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that a previously existing machine be identical in every respect to defeat a patent; the test is what is new in the mode of operation or peculiar device of producing the given effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere new purpose or effect of old apparatus is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere purpose, or effect of a machine, however novel, furnishes no ground for a valid patent unless the machine itself, the instrument by which the purpose is effected, is substantially new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application of what is old to a new purpose (without a substantial change in the instrument) is not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of ingenuity is not dispositive if invention is substantially new
rubrics_metrics.description: Provided the invention is substantially new, it is of no consequence whether a great or small amount of thought, ingenuity, skill, labor, or experiment has been expended; even accidental discovery may suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sufficiency of invention is judged by novelty/substantial difference, not by measured quantity of inventive effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention includes application of natural laws/forces as well as arrangement of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of invention embraces more than the new arrangement of particles of matter; the purpose is to produce some new effect or result by calling into activity some latent law, force, or property of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essence or principle of many inventions is the effect produced by the application of natural laws (e.g., expansive power of steam); excluding the application of a natural law from the definition of invention is erroneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature cannot be patented in the abstract; practical application may be
rubrics_metrics.description: A law, property, or rule of abstract science cannot, in the abstract, be appropriated by any man; but if an inventor for the first time produces an effect practically by the application of a law, he may appropriate that law so far as to prevent others from applying the same law to produce the same effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriation extends to the application that produces the practical effect, regardless of variations in means, apparatus, forms, or arrangements, unless such variations introduce a new law or create a substantially different result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation of known qualities or laws when applied to produce a particular effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions consisting in the application of known qualities of substances or well-known laws of physical science may involve and admit of appropriation of those qualities/laws in their application to produce a particular effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: using India rubber to give elasticity to card backs; forcing air through syrup to promote evaporation. Any person applying the same law to the same purpose, though by a different apparatus, would practise the same invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions independent of form cover equivalent variations of means
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the invention has a characteristic or aggregate of characteristics independent of particular form, method, arrangement, or apparatus, changes in form that do not affect the characteristic or purpose are immaterial — they are merely substitutions of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substituting a different contrivance that does not change the principle or characteristic of the invention is a different mode of practising the same invention; only changes producing a substantially different result are substantive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for extent of patentee's appropriation: piracy of the original invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth, law, property, or quality of matter which enters into the essence of an invention may be appropriated to the extent of every application which, according to principles of law and rules of logic, is to be deemed piracy of the original invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A jury, guided by law, determines which other applications constitute piracy; this is the guiding test of how broadly a patentee's appropriation extends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims construction: extent is for the court; intelligibility for practice is generally for the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: The first question — the extent of the claim — is universally a question for the court; the intelligibility of the description for the purposes of practice is generally a question for the jury under the direction of the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should construe patents fairly to ascertain whether the patentee has claimed anything beyond his real invention; when doubtful, presume the patentee intended to claim no more than he actually invented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against fraud; doubtful claims construed in patentee's favor (ut res magis valeat quam pereat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraud is never to be presumed; in doubtful cases the patentee is presumed to intend to claim no more than his actual invention. The maxim ut res magis valeat quam pereat guides construction toward supporting a claim if it can be done without violating principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If after fair construction doubt remains whether a claim is broader than the invention, adopt the rule favorable to the patentee; but where a claim manifestly admits of no construction but an invalidly comprehensive one, the rule does not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent protects fair fruits of actual invention, not a broader monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Law establishes no monopoly beyond the fair fruits of actual invention; it protects the real inventor in the enjoyment of what he first produced, and recognizes as substantive inventions changes introducing new characteristics, results, or advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law proceeds on encouraging inventive activity while limiting appropriation to the inventor's actual contribution; known properties and laws remain common property except as applied in the inventor's claimed subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: When specification includes old matter, two inquiries determine overclaiming
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether the patentee has included in his claim anything that existed before, inquire (1) whether he makes use of anything not new, and (2) whether that thing, according to the fair import of his language, is represented to be part of the invention claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first is a question of evidence; the second invokes principles of construction. If claim is doubtful, apply presumption against overclaiming; if claim clearly includes old matter, the patent is unsupported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent may remain valid pro tanto after real invention is ascertained
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim is broader or narrower than the real invention, provisions of the law may allow a patent to remain valid pro tanto, after the real invention of the party has been judicially ascertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mitigates harsh consequences of over- or under-claiming by allowing partial validity anchored to the actual invention.
